title: Low, High, Middle Triple
statement:
You get an array nums. Decide whether it contains three positions i < j < k, not necessarily next to each other, where the values go low, then high, then in between:

nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j]

Both comparisons are strict. Return true if such a triple exists, otherwise false.

examples.why: 3 is the low, 8 the high, and 5 lands strictly between them.
5, 9, 7 works. The positions need not be adjacent; no three neighbours here form the shape.
The last value must be strictly above the first. Equal does not count.

hints: Fix the middle position j, the high one. Which low value on its left is the best choice?

The smallest value before j is always the best low. That gives O(n²). To go faster, scan from the right and ask: for the current value as the low, what is the best possible "in between" value already seen?

Scan right to left with a decreasing stack. When a bigger value arrives, pop everything smaller than it; the largest popped value becomes the best "middle" candidate, because it has a bigger value to its left. If any later (more left) value is below that candidate, you are done.

explain.intuition:
Think of the pattern as a high value H followed later by a middle value M < H, with something lower than M before both. Scan from the right. Keep a stack of values that are decreasing from bottom to top. When a new value x arrives and is bigger than the top of the stack, every popped value has x on its left as a bigger "high". So each popped value is a valid M, and we keep the largest one in third, since a larger M is easiest to beat from below.

Now any value further left that is smaller than third completes the triple. Each value is pushed and popped at most once, so the scan is O(n). It is the same "next greater element" stack used for things like finding the next taller element in a row of cards, run in reverse.
steps: Walk i from the last index down to 0.
If nums[i] < third, return true: it is the low.
While the stack top is smaller than nums[i], pop it into third.
Push nums[i]. If the loop ends, return false.
pitfalls: Only checking three adjacent elements. The positions can be far apart, as in [5, 9, 1, 7].
Tracking a global minimum and maximum of the whole array. Order matters: the low must come before the high, and the middle after it.

solutions.title: Best low for every pair
solutions.idea: For each j, the best low is the smallest value before it. Then try every k after j.

solutions.title: Monotonic stack from the right
solutions.idea: Values popped by a bigger value to their left are valid middles; keep the largest one and look for anything smaller further left.

followups: Return the three indexes, not just true or false.
Count how many such triples exist. Which structure helps beyond O(n²)?
